about: What this member said on the floor, from the Congressional Record: their own words only, and of those the sentences that name an alignment question's phrases or make a commitment. Written by npm run record:collect (scripts/collect-record.mjs).
name: Jonathan L. Jackson

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: FOOD INSECURITY
statements.title: FOOD INSECURITY
sentences: With grocery prices continuing to rise and SNAP participation falling by more than 5.5 million people since Trump's big, beautiful bill became law, I am urging my colleagues to pass the Farm and Family Relief Act to give families and States the breathing room that they need.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: DEADLY IMMIGRATION POLICIES
statements.title: DEADLY IMMIGRATION POLICIES
sentences: He wanted to serve the United States, but after losing his temporary protected status and being held in an ICE ankle monitor, his family says he experienced deep humiliation, fear, and despair.
Children started picking on him at school for wearing an ICE monitor because they had lost their temporary protected status.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: GIVING VOICE TO DIVERSITY, EQUITY, AND INCLUSION PRINCIPLES
statements.title: GIVING VOICE TO DIVERSITY, EQUITY, AND INCLUSION PRINCIPLES
sentences: At this time, Mr. Speaker, I rise at this moment and in this Chamber to give a voice to the tens of millions of Americans who do not believe that diversity, equity, and inclusion is an offense to the spirit of America.

Regrettably, Mr. Speaker, it is also where we begin because we will let the word go forth from this time and in this place: If the Government of the United States had simply honored the 14th and 15th Amendments ratified in 1868 and in 1870 respectively, there would be no need for diversity, equity, and inclusion today because we would have fulfilled our promise and our obligation.
Congressman Cleo Fields is the co-chair and founder of the DEI Caucus.
Mr. Speaker, I yield to the gentleman from New York (Mr. Tonko), a leader on clean energy, environmental justice, and environmental policy, who has represented the capital region since 2009.

We have gone from the veiled attempts of the segregationists now to the overt racism carefully wrapped up and disguised and repackaged saying that DEI, the program that expanded opportunity, is exclusionary.
She is a national voice on gun violence, also a doctor of medical sciences and public health, who represents the great Second District of the State of Illinois.

She is a true advocate and freedom fighter for those that have been marginalized, a determined advocate for Detroit's working poor and working families, and one of the first Muslim women to serve in the United States House of Representatives.
We would like to see fewer DUI Secretaries and more DEI candidates, persons who are simply looking for equal opportunity to be included in serving our Nation.

And as the cofounder of this DEI Caucus, I must rise to declare that with respect to the issue of equal access, equal opportunity, and equal protection under the law that the government of the United States, as it is currently configured, cannot be trusted unless we have explicit laws and codify these programs to ensure a greater America.
We have been moving toward a more perfect Union, and this administration amongst all administrations has been the most hostile towards inclusivity.
To echo the words of Congressman Jamie Raskin, we have had more DUI hires in this administration's Cabinet than we have had DEI hires of those that have been qualified.
I would tell you, Mr. Speaker, we are moving toward a more perfect Union.
When we look at how do we make Canada, one of our oldest and longest and greatest political allies become a trade war partner.

We have heard my colleagues, and I have discussed, the problems we have had with the dismantling of diversity, equity, and inclusion and civil rights protections across our government and across many aspects of our society.
We will continue this fight to make sure that America fulfills its promise and its destiny.
We will fight until America is right.
We will continue to stand up to defend these relentless attacks.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: FIGHTING BACK AGAINST DISMANTLING OF VOTING RIGHTS
statements.title: FIGHTING BACK AGAINST DISMANTLING OF VOTING RIGHTS
sentences: The 15th Amendment was passed, and within 10 years, the Supreme Court had gutted its enforcement, and the Redeemers had taken back the South at the point of a rifle.

Now, the Supreme Court, in a 6-3 decision in Louisiana v. Callais, has gutted section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, has taken the spine out of the only serious legal protection that Blacks, Mexicans, women, and others have had since 1965.
This is indeed LGBTQ month, Pride Month.
Congressman Takano is the first person of the LGBTQ community and of color to openly serve in the House of Representatives.
Mr. Speaker, it is now my honor and my privilege to share this podium with an outstanding young man of Indian ancestry and of the Hindu faith.
Within a decade, follow me closely, the Supreme Court in Cruikshank, gone; the poll tax, gone; the literacy test, gone; the Grandfather Clause, gone; the White primary, gone.

It took Jimmie Lee Jackson being shot by a State trooper in February 1965; it took John Lewis and Hosea Williams and 600 people walking across the Edmund Pettus Bridge on a Sunday morning in Selma, Alabama-- walking peacefully, walking prayerfully, walking legally toward a courthouse to register to vote--and getting beaten with clubs, trampled by horses, gassed in the open air on American soil--broadcast on American television for the world to see--that is what it cost to get the Voting Rights Act passed.
I will ask them directly: What side of history do they want to be recorded on when they stood up at their town hall and talked about freedom?
I will recognize my colleagues who have spoken up, but the silence is deafening.

Mr. Speaker, as we discuss the dismantling of voting rights and how many of my colleagues and I will continue to stand up to defend our most sacred right, I am proud to be joined by my colleagues who have stood up for the right side of history.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: FARM, FOOD, AND NATIONAL SECURITY ACT OF 2026
statements.title: FARM, FOOD, AND NATIONAL SECURITY ACT OF 2026
sentences: My first amendment directs the Secretary of Agriculture to report to the Congress on the increased costs that American farmers are facing due to rising costs of diesel and fertilizer prices.
These costs are a direct result of President Trump's unilateral action to embroil the United States in a protracted war with Iran.
When diesel prices rise, it is not an abstraction.
My second amendment increases civil rights accountability for employees and officials of the United States Department of Agriculture.
We will stand with the farmers struggling under rising costs.
We will stand with the farmers seeking justice at the hands of this government.
We will stand for fairness, for accountability, and for the dignity of work.
We will not remain silent in the face of inequity and inequality.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: JACKIE ROBINSON DAY
statements.title: JACKIE ROBINSON DAY
sentences: Jackie Robinson's legacy is not a DEI to be thrown away.
Mr. Jackie Robinson was court-martialed for refusing to sit in the back of a segregated bus.

And if we are worthy of that testimony, we will remember this: that America is not measured by how well it protects the powerful, but by how fiercely it defends the dignity of all who step forward--against the odds, against the noise, against history itself--to claim their place at the plate. ____________________

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: DC CRIMINAL REFORMS TO IMMEDIATELY MAKE EVERYONE SAFE ACT
statements.title: DC CRIMINAL REFORMS TO IMMEDIATELY MAKE EVERYONE SAFE ACT
sentences: It seeks to eliminate judicial discretion to impose sentences below mandatory minimums, and would restrict vital alternatives like probation, community service, and the ability to seal the records of young adult offenders.
I urge my colleagues to stand with the residents of D.C. and against this discriminatory and hypocritical bill.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: LOWERING AGE AT WHICH A MINOR MAY BE TRIED AS ADULT FOR CERTAIN CRIMINAL OFFENSES IN DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA
statements.title: LOWERING AGE AT WHICH A MINOR MAY BE TRIED AS ADULT FOR CERTAIN CRIMINAL OFFENSES IN DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA
sentences: Mr. Speaker, I rise today in strong opposition to H.R. 5140, the D.C. Juvenile Sentencing Reform Act.
This will also have the impact of reducing the minimum age for transferring a juvenile to adult court to be tried as an adult.
They come from supporting our schools, expanding after-school programs, providing job training, and ensuring access to mental health services.
I urge my colleagues to reject this misguided and dangerous bill.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: PROVIDING FOR CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENT TO H.R. 1, ONE BIG BEAUTIFUL BILL ACT
statements.title: PROVIDING FOR CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENT TO H.R. 1, ONE BIG BEAUTIFUL BILL ACT
sentences: Mr. Speaker, I ask unanimous consent to amend the rule to make in order the amendment at the desk that protects against any cuts to Medicaid and SNAP.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: NO TAX DOLLARS FOR TERRORISTS ACT
statements.title: NO TAX DOLLARS FOR TERRORISTS ACT
sentences: However, we must do so in a way that does not further alienate those partners already reeling from the Trump administration's foreign assistance freeze, which terminated nearly all humanitarian assistance to Afghanistan, despite its compliance with U.S. law and policy.
Mr. Speaker, we urgently need more information and assurances from the Trump administration about their priorities in Afghanistan and now Iran.

The United States must continue to do everything it can to support our partners on the ground providing assistance to Afghan civilians, including women and children, while also ensuring U.S. foreign assistance isn't being diverted into the hands of the Taliban.
I rise in support of H.R. 260, and I thank my dear friend and honorable colleague, the Honorable Tim Burchett from the great State of Tennessee, for his remarks.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: SANCTION SEA PIRATES ACT OF 2025
statements.title: SANCTION SEA PIRATES ACT OF 2025
sentences: Mr. Speaker, I rise in support my bill, H.R. 1998, Sanction Sea Pirates Act.
We cannot allow violent criminals and terrorists to continue stunting the economic development of Somalia and the surrounding region.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: ENDING OF DEI PROGRAMS THROUGH EXECUTIVE ORDER
statements.title: ENDING OF DEI PROGRAMS THROUGH EXECUTIVE ORDER
sentences: This museum tells the truth, that a country founded on the promise of liberty held millions in chains . . . that the price of our Union was America's original sin.
Mr. Speaker, we are addressing the issue today of diversity, equity, and inclusion.

I speak today about the persistent and harmful attacks on diversity, equity, and inclusion policies and how these attacks, particularly under the leadership of the President of the United States, are undermining the values upon which this Nation was built.
DEI, at its core, is not just a set of policies but an embodiment of American values, values that ensure every citizen, regardless of race, gender, or background, has the opportunity to thrive.
When President Trump and his allies launched their attacks on DEI, they were not merely engaging in political rhetoric.
The attack on DEI is an attack on civil rights, the idea of an egalitarian democracy, and the constitutional ideals that undergird the very idea of America.
This rhetoric is dangerous because it fundamentally misrepresents the mission of DEI and, in doing so, misrepresents the broadest civil rights movement that has shaped this Nation.
The very principles of DEI stem from these victories.

When we attack diversity, equity, and inclusion, we erode the gains made through blood, sweat, and tears from the marches in Selma to the legislative victories in the sixties, seventies, eighties, nineties, and beyond.
To push to eliminate DEI policies is a dangerous step backward in this ongoing fight for justice and equality.
It is no accident that this movement to undermine DEI coincides with the resurgence of racism and hatred, and this rhetoric and these policies are un-American.
People with different abilities are a part of DEI.
American workers are a part of DEI.
Even women and families that need IVF, in vitro fertilization to build strong American families, are all communities that benefit from DEI initiatives.
To say nothing of the fact that ensuring the right of young people to be in leadership is what diversity and inclusion is all about.
Take, for example, the recent span of book bans across the Nation, particularly those targeting African-American authors, targeting our history, and targeting our lived experiences.

When DEI programs are eliminated, when history is whitewashed, and when Black experiences are rendered invisible, the message sent to our children is clear: Your history, your experience, and your potential does not matter.
Mr. Speaker, I find it interesting when we started this conversation about diversity, equity, and inclusion, I invited some of my other colleagues to participate.
One person asked me: Is it legal for you to discuss DEI, diversity, equity, and inclusion?

Mr. Pete Hegseth, our Secretary of Defense, needs to understand, if he would take the time to read it, that diversity is legal according to the United States Supreme Court in the Students for Fair Admissions.
When they say they are anti-DEI and then they take down the statues and remove the gravestones of Jackie Robinson, that does not help with military cohesion.
If there is one of our colleagues that is watching us in the Chamber, we invite you down so we can have a debate, a discussion on DEI and stop the polarization and racializing this.
No DEI law has been passed by the Congress.
His case right now before the United States Supreme Court, Louisiana v. Callais, is taking into account, once again, the maxim of equal protection under the law.
He gave a speech that day that I wish my Republican colleagues would take the time to listen to, and I will summarize it.
By staying true to our principles, righting injustice, and encouraging the empowerment of all, we will be an even greater nation for generations to come.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: FIGHTING VOTER SUPPRESSION
statements.title: FIGHTING VOTER SUPPRESSION
sentences: This week, the President signed an executive order requiring proof of citizenship to vote in Federal elections.
He cut off mail-in ballots unless they arrive on time as he cuts the postal workforce.
We don't have a voter fraud problem in this country.
We must pass the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act to restore what the Supreme Court gutted when it ripped out preclearance.
We must pass the Freedom to Vote Act to guarantee that every citizen, no matter the ZIP Code that they live in, their income, or ancestry, can register, vote, and be counted with dignity.
We must keep building the more perfect union that the Framers spoke out about but never completed.
We won't go back to a time when folks had to count jellybeans in jars to prove they were American enough.
We won't go back to a time when the color of your skin determined the weight of your ballot or your opportunity to have a ballot in your hand.
We won't go back to a time when power was hoarded by the few and denied to the many.
The vote is sacred, and I will not rest until every hand that reaches for a ballot is met with a promise, not with a barrier.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: SAYING GOOD-BYE TO A GIANT
statements.title: SAYING GOOD-BYE TO A GIANT
sentences: His legacy will be defined by his lifelong fight for civil rights, economic justice, and opportunity for all, but perhaps some of his most visionary work was cofounding the Congressional Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Caucus that he, Congressman Fields, and I took on together with urgency and purpose.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: RAISING A QUESTION OF THE PRIVILEGES OF THE HOUSE
statements.title: RAISING A QUESTION OF THE PRIVILEGES OF THE HOUSE
sentences: Mr. Speaker, he is a man that is standing up for those who are poor, who are left out, who have been left behind, a man that is standing up for Medicaid and Medicare.

There is a theological problem in this institution when we are more kind to those who are rich and powerful than those who are poor, when we are talking about balancing the budget off the backs of those who need healthcare, who need housing, who need food assistance, to give tax breaks to the rich.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: General Leave
statements.title: General Leave
sentences: Mr. Speaker, I rise today because in light of the President's January 6 pardons, someone has to stand up for the people who defend this building, who defend the Representatives of the United States of America, and who defend this magnificent institution.

Just the other day at the beginning of this week, the members of the Capitol Police and Metropolitan Police protected us once again as we engaged in inauguration ceremonies of the 47th President of the United States of America.
The very idea of pardoning people who violently attack police officers who were protecting the United States Capitol is anathema and should be offensive to every Member of this body.

I simply cannot think of a more disgraceful act than to disrespect the life and blood and legacy of the men and women of the Capitol Police and Metropolitan Police who in some cases literally gave their lives to protect this institution and us as Representatives.
What the 47th President of the United States has done in pardoning the people who attacked the police officers is simply wrong.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to tell the members of law enforcement who protect this building and who protect our lives that the Members of the Democratic Party see them.
What happened on January 6 was violent.
What happened on January 6 was a disgrace to the men and women who serve this institution honorably.
The people who came here on January 6--that was not a day that most people in American history know what procedurally happens here.
What happens here was supposed to be the transfer of power with the electoral college votes that we ceremoniously pass.

Before we get up and speak recklessly about a mob that violently attacked police officers, we would all be wise to consider how our words will age in years to come and whether future generations will condemn what we said or that we remained silent about this issue.
Just yesterday, in this same Chamber where the officers were defending us, insurrectionists of January 6 came in here and sat up in the gallery.
If we had known then what we know now, police should have had the day off so these people could have roamed this building freely.
We do not support the unsolicited and unwarranted disrespect extended to them by the President of the United States of America.
We shall know the truth, and the truth shall set us all free.
We shall know the truth, and the truth shall set us free.
I pray that we will answer this call.
I pray we will not dishonor what is right.
I pray we will stand up for those who consistently stand up for us.
